name: Mandarin moustache

lead: The Mandarin moustache is a long, narrow moustache that starts under the nose and hangs down in thin tendrils past the corners of the mouth, often below the jawline. It is closely related to the Fu Manchu moustache, which has long, downward-pointing ends generally beyond the chin [1].
It draws the eye down the face and elongates it, and it is used as a statement style. It takes time to grow and shape.

paras: Wearers grow the moustache long while keeping the cheeks and chin shaved or kept short, and train and groom the ends so they hang straight.
The main risk is social: the Fu Manchu style has been used in caricatures of Chinese and East Asian people, and some viewers may read it that way [2].

chain: Ends hang past mouth and jaw
angle.text: A grown, groomed moustache changes how the lower face reads. The long vertical lines draw the eye downward for a dramatic, lengthened look.

lead: The Mandarin moustache is a long drooping moustache with thin hanging ends. Wikipedia describes the related Fu Manchu style as a moustache from under the nose past the corners of the mouth, hanging in two tapered tendrils often below the jaw [1].
It is used as a distinctive grooming choice: the vertical lines lengthen the lower face and give a dramatic silhouette.
The Fu Manchu style takes its name from the fictional character and became a staple of film villains; it is a competition category at the World Beard and Moustache Championships [1].

paras: The style is a long moustache without a thick horseshoe shape; unlike the horseshoe, it hangs over the jaw rather than along the sides of the mouth, and a true Fu Manchu is harder and slower to grow [1]. Wikipedia lists Fu Manchu among named moustache styles with long downward-pointing ends beyond the chin [2].
The Fu Manchu look first appeared in the British serial The Mystery of Dr. Fu Manchu in 1929, though the Sax Rohmer character had no moustache in the books; Christopher Lee wore it in 1965 [1].
Wikipedia notes the style is often used to stereotype Chinese and East Asian people, and 19th and early 20th century caricatures depicted Chinese men with it [1].
